name: Nasal saline rinse / neti pot

card.summary: Rinsing the nose with salt water to clear mucus; evidence supports temporary symptom relief in some conditions, and unsafe water has caused rare fatal infections.
card.aka: Neti pot, nasal irrigation, jala neti, nasal lavage
card.note: Tap water must be boiled, filtered or sterile per the FDA and CDC; rare fatal amoebic infections have followed tap-water use.

quick.overview:
Nasal irrigation rinses mucus and debris from the nose and sinuses using saline from a neti pot, squeeze bottle, bulb syringe or electric device. It has roots in Ayurvedic practice (jala neti) and is used in looksmaxxing circles to reduce allergic congestion.

Reviews cited on Wikipedia report it can relieve acute sinusitis symptoms, may temporarily help allergic rhinitis, and has weak evidence in chronic sinusitis. Appearance effects (such as less congestion-related puffiness) were not examined.
quick.mechanism: A saline stream flushes mucus, allergens and debris out of the nasal passages. Studies of devices find sinus penetration differs by device, head position and anatomy.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally mild: irritation, nosebleeds, headache. Rare fatal infections with Naegleria fowleri followed neti-pot use with tap water (including two deaths in 2011), and the FDA warned in 2017 that improper use can be harmful. The CDC advises boiled, filtered (NSF 53/58 or 1 micron), sterile or distilled, or disinfected water.

lead: Nasal irrigation, also called nasal lavage or, with the vessel, a neti pot, is a hygiene practice that rinses mucus and debris from the nose and sinuses. It is traced to Ayurveda, where jala neti (water) and sutra neti (string) were part of personal hygiene [1].

Evidence summarised on Wikipedia indicates irrigation can relieve acute sinusitis symptoms from upper respiratory infections, may temporarily relieve allergic rhinitis symptoms, and has weak support in chronic sinusitis [1]. It is generally well tolerated, with irritation, nosebleeds and headache reported [1].
Untreated tap water has been linked to rare fatal infections, and the FDA and CDC give guidance on water safety [1].
infobox: Neti pot, squeeze bottle, bulb syringe, electric irrigator
Acute sinusitis: relief; allergic rhinitis: temporary relief; chronic sinusitis: weak

paras: Neti pots use gravity and head position; squeeze bottles apply the fluid by hand; bulb syringes are common for infants; electric machines use pumps [1]. Saline is the common solution, and some irrigations carry added medications such as budesonide for chronic rhinosinusitis [1].

A cadaver study found sinus distribution of solutions differed among pressurized spray, neti pot and squeeze bottle, and varied after endoscopic sinus surgery [2]. A 3D-printed model study reported that penetration is variable and depends on the individual's anatomy and technique variables such as head position and flow rate [3]. Reviews describe irrigation as an adjunct after endoscopic sinus surgery [4].

Tap water may contain microbes harmless to drink but dangerous in the nose. Wikipedia reports two deaths in 2011 tied to neti pots filled with tap water, a 2013 Louisiana death from the same amoeba, and a 2018 Balamuthia mandrillaris infection after a month of tap water filtered through a household purifier [1].

The FDA stated on January 24, 2017 that improper use can be harmful. The CDC lists four water options: boiling for one minute then cooling, filtering with an NSF 53 or 58 device or an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller, buying distilled or sterile water, or disinfecting with chlorine bleach [1]. A case report describes Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis associated with over-the-counter sinus irrigation [5].

The practice appears in appearance discussions as a way to reduce allergic congestion, which proponents link to dark circles and facial puffiness. The source reviewed contains no research on that appearance link.

No studies found on appearance outcomes. For symptoms, a systematic review and meta-analysis (Hermelingmeier et al., 2012) and a 2016 Cochrane review are cited on Wikipedia for allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis respectively [1].

timeline.event: Two deaths tied to neti pots filled with tap water are reported. [1]
FDA warns that improper neti-pot use can be harmful (January 24). [1]
